name: 肉うどん さんすけ (Niku Udon Sansuke)

claims.text: Wheat noodles are the restaurant's entire product; flour is present throughout the kitchen. No gluten-free alternative exists and cross-contamination is unavoidable.

The broth uses Imokei tamari soy sauce from Gifu Prefecture. Tamari is typically made with little or no wheat, but this has not been confirmed as certified gluten-free and is served in a wheat-noodle kitchen.
Pork chashu, chicken oil, and animal dashi are core broth components. There is no vegan path through the menu.
Staff are noted as patient and thorough in explaining the menu to first-time visitors, but no allergy or dietary accommodation protocols have been documented by any source.
No information about kitchen separation or cross-contamination controls is publicly available. The tearoom is a small traditional operation with no allergen documentation found online.

No soy sauce-based dishes appear on the menu. The menu is limited to matcha, wagashi sweets, and mitsumame — soy sauce is not a standard ingredient in any of these. However, wagashi recipes are not disclosed and hidden wheat starch in confections cannot be ruled out.
No dairy or egg dishes visible on the menu alongside the matcha and wagashi offerings, but no formal separation protocol confirmed.
No information found regarding staff allergy training or allergy-aware ordering procedures. The tearoom is a compact, city-run facility without documented allergy protocols.

The core menu — plain matcha and mitsumame (agar jelly, sweet azuki beans, fruit) — uses ingredients that are traditionally wheat-free, dairy-free, and meat-free, making incidental safety plausible for those with moderate sensitivities.
Menu is short and simple (matcha, wagashi, mitsumame), reducing the number of unknowns compared to a full kitchen restaurant.

name: 濃厚中華そば 佐とう (Noko Chuka Soba Sato)

claims.text: No gluten-free accommodations exist. Wheat noodles are the core product cooked in the same kitchen, making cross-contamination certain.
Broth is seasoned with tamari soy sauce; tamari in Japanese commercial production frequently contains trace wheat, and no wheat-free tamari claim is made.
All broth is pork-based; no plant-based or separate cooking line exists.
No allergy-handling protocols or allergen menus are mentioned on any source reviewed. Phone lines are closed during service hours.

name: 美味しいごはん じらふ (Oishii Gohan Jirafu)

claims.text: Kushiage (deep-fried skewers) is a core menu category using four types of breadcrumbs, almost certainly wheat-based. The fryer is very likely shared with other fried items including karaage. No dedicated fryer information found.

The signature yakibuta dish uses a soy-based tare that has been maintained since opening. Standard Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu) contains wheat. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.
Pork, chicken, and egg dishes dominate the menu. The frying oil is shared with animal-based kushiage. No vegan-safe cooking zones or oils confirmed.

The owner-chef accepts off-menu requests when ingredients are available, suggesting some flexibility, but no allergy protocol or dietary accommodation system is described on any public source. Communication in Japanese is essential.
Owner-chef with 20+ years of experience runs a small, personal kitchen — direct communication about dietary needs is more feasible than at a chain restaurant.

name: 大銀杏 名古屋西店 (Ooicho Nagoya Nishi-ten)

claims.text: No dedicated GF kitchen or allergen separation is documented. Shared charcoal grill used for all skewers including tare-marinated items.

Tare (sweet soy-based glaze) used on standard yakitori skewers contains wheat. Shio (salt-grilled) option uses housemade salt from bonito and kombu dashi; wheat-free status of this salt is unconfirmed.
All skewers are animal-based and the grill is entirely shared. Bonito-kombu salt is used across the menu. No vegan-safe items identified.
No allergen menu or allergy handling policy is listed on any available source. Phone inquiry (052-325-5626) before visiting is strongly advised for any dietary restriction.

Charcoal grilling rather than deep-frying eliminates shared-fryer cross-contamination risk. Shio (salt-only) skewers avoid tare sauce for those avoiding soy; ask staff to confirm which skewers can be ordered shio.

name: オステリア オルモ (Osteria OLMO)

claims.text: 専用グルテンフリー調理器具・フライヤーの分離使用に関する情報は公式サイト・各種レビューとも一切記載なし。パスタ・セモリナ粉・小麦フリットを多用するキッチンでの交差汚染リスクは高いと考えられる。
醤油・だし（小麦含有の可能性）の使用有無についての情報は公開されていない。イタリア料理が主体だが、日本の旬食材を多用するため隠し味として使用している可能性を排除できない。
乳製品（ストラッチャテッラ、ゴートチーズ等）・魚介・肉を同一キッチンで扱う。ヴィーガン専用調理ラインの情報なし。
「アレルギーや苦手食材は2日前までにお知らせいただければ対応します」と案内されている（食べログ情報）。対応の具体的範囲（代替食材の内容・除去の確実性等）は不明。セリアックや重篤なアレルギーの方は予約時に直接詳細を確認することを強く推奨。
完全予約制のため、事前にアレルギー・食材の希望を伝える機会が確保されている。少人数制（15席）で、シェフが一人ひとりの状況に配慮しやすい環境。

name: オステリア オルカドーロ (Osteria Orca d'Oro)

claims.text: Fresh handmade wheat pasta is a core menu item and flour is in active use throughout service; cross-contamination cannot be ruled out without direct confirmation from the kitchen.
No soy sauce-based preparations are documented for this Italian kitchen, but standard wheat-containing Italian ingredients (pasta dough, bread, flour-dusted proteins) are present throughout the menu.

Butter, cream, fish stock, and cured meats are standard components of an Italian osteria kitchen; vegan cross-contact from shared surfaces and cookware is expected unless the kitchen is asked to accommodate a specific order separately.

No allergen protocol, allergy menu, or staff allergy-handling procedure has been documented in any public source reviewed. The restaurant does note it will try to accommodate guest requests, but this is framed around taste preferences, not food safety.

Chef adapts dishes to guest preferences on request — guests with dietary needs who call ahead may be able to arrange a custom plate, as the menu is inherently flexible and not bound to a printed list.

name: 尾張 粋 稲葉 (Owari Sui Inaba)

claims.text: The tempura counter uses wheat-flour batter as a core element of every course; cross-contamination with shared kitchen equipment is highly likely.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is used throughout the kappo menu for seasoning, sauces, and marinades — no gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Fish dashi (bonito/kombu) is foundational to the kappo cuisine style; plant-based dashi is not indicated anywhere in the menu descriptions.
The restaurant requires allergy disclosure before the visit and states it may decline to accommodate requests in order to prioritize guest safety; same-day changes are not possible.
Allergy information is formally collected at reservation stage, giving the kitchen advance notice to plan or decline gracefully.
